opus-5.5.text:
I usually think about it as a kind of pyramid, organized by how directly the data relates to the robot you actually care about.

At the top is real-robot data, mostly collected through teleoperation. A person drives the robot with a VR headset, a puppeteering rig, or a spacemouse, and you record the observations and actions. This is the gold standard because there's no embodiment gap: it's exactly the robot, the sensors, and the action space you'll deploy with. The problem is cost. It scales roughly linearly with human hours and hardware, so even the biggest efforts, the Open X-Embodiment-style pooled datasets, are tiny compared to what vision or language models train on.

In the middle is simulation and synthetic data. You can generate an enormous amount of it, run reinforcement learning, randomize everything, and use procedural generation or even generative models to create scenes and trajectories. In principle it's nearly free to scale. The catch is the sim-to-real gap: contact physics, deformables, and visual realism are still hard. Also, someone has to build the tasks and assets, so it's less free than it looks. Things like locomotion transfer well; contact-rich manipulation is harder.

At the bottom, and by far the largest, is human and internet data: videos of people doing things, egocentric recordings, YouTube, and the language and image data inside pretrained foundation models. This is where the general knowledge lives, like what objects are, how people interact with them, and what a sensible plan for a task looks like. But it has no robot actions in it, and human hands aren't robot grippers, so you have to bridge an embodiment gap and infer action information somehow.

A lot of my group's work, and where I think the field is heading, sits between those layers. One example is collecting human data in a more structured way, using wearable devices or handheld grippers that make a human demonstration look closer to robot data. That way you get much of the scale of human data and much of the usefulness of robot data. So the real research question isn't which category wins. It's how to build a data recipe that mixes all three: using the broad, cheap data for priors and the small amount of expensive, on-robot data to ground everything in the actual embodiment.

r001.rationale: The response groups videos, egocentric recordings, and YouTube under human and internet data, then mentions structured wearable or handheld-gripper demonstrations. It does not clearly distinguish unconstrained internet downloads from deliberately collected first-person human hand-manipulation recordings as two types.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. The way I usually think about it, there are roughly three buckets, and they trade off against each other along one axis: how much the data looks like what the robot will actually experience at deployment, versus how much of it you can get.

The first bucket is real robot data, collected on the physical hardware. The gold standard here is teleoperation, where a human drives the robot through a task and you record the observations and actions. That data is exactly in-distribution: right sensors, right embodiment, right physics. The problem is it's expensive and slow. You need a person, a robot, a scene, and time, and every demonstration costs you minutes. Efforts like Open X-Embodiment or DROID are attempts to pool this across labs, but we're still talking about on the order of a million trajectories at best, which is tiny by the standards of language or vision.

The second bucket is simulation data. You build a virtual environment, and now the robot can run millions of trials in parallel, you can randomize physics and lighting, and you can generate demonstrations with planners or scripted policies instead of humans. We've done a lot of work in this space, things like MimicGen, where you take a handful of human demos and automatically synthesize thousands of variations. The catch is the sim-to-real gap. Contact physics, deformables, visual realism, all of it is approximate, and policies can overfit to the simulator's quirks.

The third bucket is what I'd call human data or internet-scale data: egocentric video of people doing tasks, YouTube, large vision-language corpora. It's essentially unlimited and it captures enormous diversity of objects, scenes, and behaviors. But it's not robot data. There are no robot actions, the embodiment is different, and the camera isn't where your robot's camera is. So you use it for pretraining representations, for learning world models or affordances, or for teaching the model semantic grounding, rather than directly for control.

A fourth thing I'd mention, which cuts across the others, is autonomous or on-policy data: the robot collecting its own experience through reinforcement learning or self-supervised play. That's in some sense the dream, because the robot becomes its own data engine, but it's hard to make safe and efficient in the real world.

So the research question I find most interesting isn't really which bucket is best. It's how you compose them: use internet data for priors, simulation for scale and diversity, and a small amount of real robot data to anchor everything to the actual hardware.

r001.rationale: The response groups egocentric video, YouTube, and vision-language corpora into one human-data bucket. It does not distinguish unconstrained internet downloads from deliberately collected first-person hand-manipulation recordings.

astra-6.text:
I’d put them into three broad categories. The first is data collected directly on robots—things like human demonstrations through teleoperation, or experience a robot gathers by trying things itself. That gives you observations, actions, and outcomes tied to the robot’s actual embodiment.

The second is simulation data. You can generate a lot of experience and vary objects, environments, and tasks, but you still have to bridge the gap between simulation and the real world.

The third is data that wasn’t collected on robots at all: images, text, and especially videos of humans doing things. That can give a model broad knowledge about the world and what tasks look like, but it usually doesn’t tell you exactly which robot actions to take.

So a big question is how to combine that broad, abundant data with the much more specific experience a robot needs to actually act.

r001.rationale: The response groups non-robot data as images, text, and human videos, but does not distinguish unconstrained internet downloads from deliberately collected first-person human hand-manipulation recordings.

sol-6.1.text:
I’d roughly divide it into three categories. The first is data collected on real robots—things like human teleoperation demonstrations or experience the robot gathers itself. That’s directly relevant to the task, but it can be expensive and slow to collect.

The second is simulation data. You can generate a lot of experience in parallel, with more control over the environment, but there’s a gap between what works in simulation and what works in the real world.

The third is data that wasn’t collected with a robot at all: human videos, images, and text. There’s a huge amount of that available, and it can teach a model about objects, tasks, and how the world works. The challenge is translating that knowledge into actions a robot can actually execute. A lot of robot learning today is about finding ways to combine those three sources.

r001.rationale: The response mentions non-robot data such as human videos, images, and text, but does not distinguish unconstrained internet downloads from deliberately collected first-person hand-manipulation recordings.
